title: OEE

breakdowns.name: Breakdowns
breakdowns.meaning: The machine stopped because something failed: a motor, a sensor, a seal bar. Each breakdown takes the whole run time with it, and the same failures tend to return.
moves: List the breakdowns of the last two weeks by component; the top one gets a 5 Whys this week.
Agree a reaction standard: who is called after how many minutes, and what the operator checks first.
Add the failing part to daily operator care: clean, inspect, tighten, with a tick on the machine.
breakdowns.question: Which part failed most often, and what did it look like one shift before?

setup.name: Setup and adjustments
setup.meaning: Changeovers, adjustments and the start-up after a change: the time from the last good piece of one order to the first good piece of the next.
moves: Film one changeover and split it into steps the machine must be stopped for and steps that can be done while it runs.
Prepare tools, film and settings before the stop: a changeover cart with a checklist.
Write the settings of each product on the machine, so nobody adjusts by trial and error.
setup.question: Which steps of the changeover could be done before the machine stops?

smallStops.name: Small stops
smallStops.meaning: Jams, misfeeds, a blocked outfeed: stops of a minute or two that the operator clears without calling anyone. One by one they look harmless; together they eat an hour.
moves: Count the small stops of one shift with a tally sheet at the machine, by place.
Fix the top jam point with the operator and maintenance together, not with a workaround.
Check the infeed: an uneven flow of parcels or packs starts most jams.
smallStops.question: Where on the machine does the operator reach in most often?

speed.name: Reduced speed
speed.meaning: The machine runs, but slower than its ideal rate: set down after a problem and never set back, or running at the pace of the slowest product.
moves: Compare the set speed with the ideal rate on the machine plate and in the settings; write down why they differ.
Raise the speed in steps of 5 % on one shift and watch rejects and jams.
Find out what the machine waits for: the infeed, the outfeed or the operator.
speed.question: Why does the machine run at this speed, and who decided it?

startupRejects.name: Startup rejects
startupRejects.meaning: Bad pieces made while the machine warms up or after a changeover, before the settings are stable.
moves: For one week, count the rejects of the first 15 minutes apart from the rest.
Write down the start-up settings of each product and check them before the first piece.
Warm up the parts that need it (seal bars, glue) before the shift starts.
startupRejects.question: How many pieces does it take until the first good one, and why that many?

productionRejects.name: Production rejects
productionRejects.meaning: Bad pieces in stable running: misreads, missorts, weak seals, damage. Each one used machine time and must be made again.
moves: Sort the rejects of one shift by defect type; the biggest one gets a check at the machine.
Show the reject count at the machine every hour, so the operator sees a change at once.
Check the input: many rejects come from labels, packaging or material, not from the machine.
productionRejects.question: What does a typical reject look like, and where was it made?

verdicts.name: World class
verdicts.note: 85 % or more: availability, performance and quality all near their best.

verdicts.name: Typical
verdicts.note: 60 to 85 %: a usual result, with clear losses to win back.

verdicts.name: Low
verdicts.note: 40 to 60 %: large losses; the biggest one is worth a project of its own.

verdicts.name: Poor
verdicts.note: Under 40 %: check the data first, then the biggest loss.

placeholders.note: e.g. Film from the new supplier

tips: Its OEE is the output of the whole line. Measure one machine well before you measure all of them.
Write the reason, not only the minutes.
A stop without a reason cannot be fixed. Keep the list of reasons short and the same on every shift.
Use the ideal rate from the machine plate.
Not the speed it usually runs at. When performance shows 100 %, the ideal rate is probably set too low.
Breaks, meetings and no orders are taken out of the planned time, so OEE measures only the time the machine was meant to run.
